title: Economic History and History of Economic Thought
topics: Pre-industrial economies and the Great Divergence
The first globalisation and the gold standard
The interwar years and the Great Depression
Classical economists: Smith, Ricardo, Malthus, Marx

notes.h: Pre-industrial economies and the Great Divergence
notes.body:
Before about 1800, most of the world lived close to subsistence. In the Malthusian model, higher incomes raise fertility and lower mortality, so population grows until wages fall back; technical progress raises population density, not living standards, in the long run. Clark (A Farewell to Alms, 2007) argues that this trap held almost everywhere until the Industrial Revolution.

Not quite stagnant. Historians stress growth episodes within the pre-industrial world:
- Smithian growth from specialisation and market integration (for example the Dutch Golden Age and Song China).
- After the Black Death (1347–51), real wages in western Europe rose sharply as labour became scarce.
- The "Little Divergence": by the 17th–18th centuries, real wages in London and Amsterdam stayed well above those in southern and central Europe (Allen, 2001), and the North Sea economies grew richer.
- De Vries's "industrious revolution": households worked longer and more for the market to buy new consumer goods before mechanisation.

The Great Divergence. The term is Pomeranz's (The Great Divergence, 2000). He argued that the Yangzi delta and England were broadly comparable in living standards and market development as late as about 1750, and that Britain's breakthrough owed much to accessible coal and to the "ghost acres" of the New World, which relieved land constraints. This "California School" view (with Wong and others) challenged older Eurocentric explanations.

Critics using new data push the divergence earlier. Broadberry and co-authors reconstruct GDP per head showing China falling behind England and Holland from the 17th century or earlier; Allen's wage comparisons put Yangzi delta living standards below England's by the 18th century, though closer to the rest of Europe.

Competing explanations
- Institutions: constraints on the executive, secure property rights and the effects of Atlantic trade on merchant power (North and Weingast, 1989; Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson, 2005).
- Culture and ideas: Mokyr's "culture of growth" (Mokyr received half of the 2025 Nobel prize, shared with Aghion and Howitt) and the Republic of Letters; McCloskey's "bourgeois dignity".
- State competition and fragmentation in Europe versus a unified Chinese empire.
- Factor prices: high wages and cheap energy in Britain (Allen, 2009).

Applied illustration. Post-1350 England: population fell by perhaps a third or more, the land–labour ratio rose, and real wages of labourers roughly doubled over the following century, consistent with Malthusian logic.

Exam pitfalls
- Treating "pre-industrial" as uniform stagnation.
- Assuming Pomeranz claims China and Europe were equal everywhere: his comparison is of core regions.
- Confusing the Little Divergence (within Europe) with the Great Divergence (Europe vs Asia).

The British Industrial Revolution (roughly 1760–1840) marked the transition to sustained increases in output per head through mechanisation, inanimate power and new forms of organisation.

Key innovations
- Textiles: Hargreaves's spinning jenny (c.1764), Arkwright's water frame (patented 1769) and factory system, Crompton's mule (1779); cotton output soared.
- Power: Newcomen's atmospheric engine (1712); Watt's separate condenser (patented 1769) improved efficiency, but steam overtook water power in British industry only in the 1830s.
- Iron: Darby's coke smelting (1709) and Cort's puddling and rolling process (1784).
- Transport: canals from the 1760s; railways after the Liverpool and Manchester Railway (1830).

Pace. Older views pictured a sudden "take-off" (Rostow, 1960). Crafts and Harley's revisions in the 1980s showed that aggregate growth was slow: output per head grew well under 1% a year before 1830, because modernising sectors such as cotton were a small share of a largely traditional economy. TFP growth was modest. Yet change was revolutionary in structure: the share of the labour force in agriculture fell markedly and Britain became the first predominantly urban industrial nation.

Why Britain?
- Allen's high-wage, cheap-energy hypothesis (2009): high wages and cheap coal made labour-saving, energy-using machines profitable in Britain first; later improvements made them viable elsewhere.
- Mokyr's Industrial Enlightenment: a culture linking science, artisans and practical knowledge; propositional knowledge fed into techniques.
- Institutions after the Glorious Revolution of 1688 (North and Weingast, 1989), though critics note property rights were already secure.
- Coal endowments (Wrigley's shift from an organic to a mineral economy), empire and Atlantic trade, agricultural productivity and enclosure.

Living standards debate. Optimists versus pessimists: Feinstein (1998) found real wages rose only slowly until the 1830s–40s; Allen (2009) describes "Engels' pause", when output per worker grew but real wages stagnated, raising the profit share. Heights, mortality in growing cities and child labour complicate the picture.

Applied illustration. In cotton spinning, the labour hours needed to process 100 lb of cotton fell by orders of magnitude between hand spinning and powered mules, so the price of cotton yarn collapsed, transforming a single sector while aggregate growth remained modest.

Exam pitfalls
- Equating dramatic sectoral change with rapid aggregate growth.
- Overstating steam's early role.
- Presenting Allen and Mokyr as mutually exclusive: many accounts combine demand for inventions (incentives) with supply (knowledge).

notes.h: The first globalisation and the classical gold standard
notes.body:
Between about 1870 and 1914 the world economy integrated as never before. Falling transport costs (steamships, railways, the Suez Canal in 1869, refrigeration) and the telegraph drove commodity price convergence. O'Rourke and Williamson (Globalization and History, 1999) show that the wheat price gap between Liverpool and Chicago narrowed sharply, while mass migration of tens of millions of Europeans to the New World narrowed wage gaps between the Old and New Worlds.

Distributional effects followed Heckscher–Ohlin logic: European landowners lost from cheap grain imports while workers gained; in land-abundant economies landowners gained. Responses differed: Britain stayed with free trade, while Germany (Bismarck's 1879 tariff), France (Méline tariff, 1892) and the USA raised protection. Rising immigration restrictions foreshadowed the backlash after 1914.

Capital flows. Britain exported capital on a huge scale; by 1913 its net foreign assets exceeded a year's GDP, much of it in railways and government bonds of the Americas and empire. Whether this starved British domestic industry of investment remains debated.

The classical gold standard. Britain had been effectively on gold since the 18th century and formally from 1816–21 (convertibility resumed in 1821); most major economies joined in the 1870s (Germany 1871–73, US de facto 1879). Each currency was convertible at a fixed gold price, so exchange rates were fixed within narrow "gold points".

Adjustment mechanisms
- Hume's price-specie-flow mechanism (1752): a deficit country loses gold, money and prices fall, competitiveness improves.
- In practice, capital flows and Bank Rate did much of the work; the "rules of the game" (Keynes's later phrase) were often broken, as central banks sterilised flows.
- Credibility: commitment to convertibility meant that capital flowed stabilisingly when a currency weakened. Eichengreen (Golden Fetters, 1992) stresses credibility and cooperation among central banks, underpinned by limited political pressure from labour.
- The system was centred on London and sterling; Bank of England reserves were remarkably small.

In trilemma terms, the gold standard combined fixed rates and capital mobility at the cost of monetary autonomy. Periphery economies faced sharper adjustment and more frequent crises (Argentina's Baring crisis of 1890).

Applied illustration. A rise in Bank Rate attracted short-term capital to London within days, stabilising sterling far faster than goods-price adjustment would.

Exam pitfalls
- Describing the gold standard as automatic.
- Assuming globalisation was irreversible: it collapsed after 1914.
- Forgetting the political economy of who gained and lost.

notes.h: The interwar years and the Great Depression
notes.body:
The First World War ended the classical gold standard. Postwar Europe faced war debts, reparations under the Treaty of Versailles (1919) and hyperinflation in Germany (peaking in 1923) and Austria, Hungary and Poland. Keynes's Economic Consequences of the Peace (1919) attacked reparations as unworkable.

The gold-exchange standard. Britain returned to gold at the prewar parity of $4.86 in 1925 under Churchill; Keynes argued sterling was overvalued by around 10%. France returned in 1926–28 at an undervalued rate and accumulated gold. The restored system was fragile: reserves were scarce and maldistributed, with France and the US sterilising inflows; cooperation was weak; and workers' political power made deflation harder.

The Great Depression. From 1929 to 1933 US industrial production fell by roughly half, real GNP by over a quarter and unemployment peaked near a quarter of the labour force. World trade collapsed.

Explanations
- Monetary: Friedman and Schwartz (A Monetary History of the United States, 1963) blamed the Fed for allowing the money stock to fall by about a third amid banking panics from 1930 onwards.
- Credit and financial: Bernanke (1983) showed bank failures destroyed lending relationships; Fisher's debt deflation amplified the slump.
- Gold standard: Eichengreen (1992) and Temin argued that the gold standard transmitted deflation internationally and stopped countries reflating. Countries that left earlier recovered earlier (Eichengreen and Sachs, 1985): Britain left in September 1931; the US devalued in 1933–34; the Gold Bloc, led by France, held on until 1936 and suffered longest.
- Demand: Temin emphasised an autonomous fall in spending; the 1929 stock market crash hit wealth and confidence.
- Trade policy: the Smoot–Hawley tariff (1930) invited retaliation, though most economists see it as a secondary cause.

Recovery. Leaving gold allowed monetary expansion. In Britain, cheap money from 1932 supported a housing boom. The US New Deal combined banking reform (Glass–Steagall Act and deposit insurance in 1933) with relief and public works, but fiscal stimulus was modest relative to the output gap. Premature tightening in 1937 caused a sharp recession.

Applied illustration. Sweden left gold in 1931 and adopted an explicit price-level objective, an early forerunner of inflation targeting, and recovered relatively well.

Exam pitfalls
- Treating the 1929 crash as the sole cause.
- Ignoring the international dimension and the timing of exits from gold.
- Overstating the New Deal's fiscal stance.

Western Europe and Japan grew at historically unprecedented rates between about 1950 and 1973. Maddison's estimates show western European GDP per head growing at around 4% a year and Japan's at about 8%, compared with under 2% for most earlier periods. The US grew more slowly, so others converged towards it.

Bretton Woods (1944). Currencies were pegged to the dollar, which was convertible into gold at $35 per ounce for official holders; parities were adjustable in cases of "fundamental disequilibrium". Capital controls were permitted, so countries kept monetary autonomy: in trilemma terms they gave up capital mobility. The IMF provided short-term finance and the World Bank long-term lending. Full current-account convertibility in western Europe came only in 1958.

Why so fast?
- Catch-up and convergence: Europe was far behind the US technological frontier, so it could import technology and organisational methods (Abramovitz, 1986, on "social capability"; Gerschenkron on relative backwardness).
- Structural change: labour moved out of low-productivity agriculture into industry (Kindleberger's labour surplus).
- High investment and social contracts: Eichengreen argues that corporatist bargains traded wage moderation for investment.
- Trade liberalisation: GATT (1947) rounds, the European Payments Union (1950) and the EEC (Treaty of Rome, 1957).
- Marshall Aid (1948–52): modest relative to recipients' national income (a few per cent a year), but DeLong and Eichengreen argue it mattered by supporting market-oriented policies and stabilisation.

Britain's relative decline. UK growth (about 2.5% a year per head) was respectable but slower than its neighbours'. Explanations include less room to catch up, stop–go demand management under a balance-of-payments constraint, fragmented industrial relations, weak management and training, and missed early EEC membership.

The end of Bretton Woods. Triffin's dilemma (1960): the world needed growing dollar liquidity, but rising US liabilities undermined confidence in gold convertibility. US inflation, Vietnam war spending and persistent deficits led Nixon to close the gold window in August 1971. The Smithsonian Agreement failed, and generalised floating began in 1973. The first oil shock (1973) and productivity slowdown ended the golden age.

Applied illustration. Sterling's devaluation from $2.80 to $2.40 in 1967 showed the strain of defending pegs under growing capital mobility.

Exam pitfalls
- Crediting Marshall Aid alone.
- Treating the golden age as a uniquely policy-driven miracle and ignoring catch-up.
- Saying Bretton Woods ended in 1971 alone: floating became general in 1973.

After 1973 the advanced economies faced stagflation. The oil shocks of 1973 and 1979, a productivity slowdown and rising inflation discredited fine-tuning. The Volcker Fed (from 1979) and Thatcher government (from 1979) squeezed inflation out at high cost in unemployment; monetarist targets for money growth were soon abandoned as velocity proved unstable.

The second globalisation. Trade liberalisation through GATT rounds culminated in the Uruguay Round and the World Trade Organization (1995). Capital controls were removed (the UK in 1979; the EU's single market in capital by 1990). Container shipping and information technology cut costs. China's reform from 1978 and WTO accession in 2001, India's 1991 reforms and the collapse of the Soviet bloc brought billions of workers into world markets. The "Washington Consensus" (Williamson's 1989 term) summarised a package of liberalising reforms promoted for developing countries.

Crises
- Latin American debt crisis (from Mexico's moratorium in 1982): petrodollar lending at floating rates became unpayable when US rates rose; the region's "lost decade" ended with the Brady Plan (1989).
- ERM crisis (1992): sterling left the Exchange Rate Mechanism on 16 September 1992 ("Black Wednesday") under speculative attack, as German interest rates rose after reunification; a classic second-generation crisis. The UK adopted inflation targeting in October 1992.
- Mexico's tequila crisis (1994–95).
- Asian financial crisis (1997–98): Thailand floated the baht in July 1997; contagion spread to Indonesia, Korea and Malaysia. Causes included short-term foreign-currency borrowing, weak banks and pegs. IMF programmes requiring fiscal austerity and high interest rates were criticised by Stiglitz and others. Malaysia imposed capital controls.
- Russia's default and the failure of Long-Term Capital Management (1998); Argentina's currency board collapse (2001–02).

Interpretation. These crises fuelled debate on capital-account liberalisation; the IMF later (2012) accepted that capital-flow management could be appropriate in some circumstances. Emerging economies accumulated reserves as self-insurance, contributing to "global imbalances" before 2008. Rodrik's globalisation trilemma holds that deep economic integration, national sovereignty and democracy cannot all be fully achieved together.

Applied illustration. A Thai firm borrowing in dollars to finance baht-earning property saw the baht value of its debt roughly double when the baht fell from about 25 to about 50 per dollar, illustrating balance-sheet effects.

Exam pitfalls
- Treating all crises as identical: distinguish fiscal, self-fulfilling and balance-sheet causes.
- Assuming liberalisation was uniformly harmful or beneficial: East Asian success and crisis coexisted.

notes.h: Classical political economy: Smith, Ricardo, Malthus, Marx
notes.body:
Adam Smith (1723–90). The Wealth of Nations (1776) argued that wealth is the annual produce of land and labour, not stocks of gold, and attacked mercantilism.
- The division of labour, illustrated by the pin factory, raises productivity, but is "limited by the extent of the market".
- Self-interest in competitive markets can promote the public good; the "invisible hand" phrase appears only once in the book, in the context of investing domestically. Smith also wrote The Theory of Moral Sentiments (1759) on sympathy and moral judgement.
- He defended natural liberty but supported roles for the state in defence, justice, public works and education, and warned that merchants' meetings tend to end in conspiracies against the public.

David Ricardo (1772–1823). Principles of Political Economy and Taxation (1817).
- Comparative advantage: England and Portugal both gain by specialising (cloth and wine) even if Portugal is more productive in both.
- Theory of rent: differential rent arises as cultivation extends to less fertile land; with population growth, rents rise and profits are squeezed, leading to a stationary state.
- Opposed the Corn Laws, which protected landlords; they were repealed in 1846.
- Labour theory of value (with acknowledged qualifications) and Ricardian equivalence (which he raised but doubted).

Thomas Malthus (1766–1834). An Essay on the Principle of Population (1798): population tends to grow geometrically while subsistence grows arithmetically, so "positive checks" (famine, disease) and "preventive checks" (later marriage) limit growth. He also argued, against Say's law and Ricardo, that general gluts of unsold goods were possible, a point Keynes praised.

Karl Marx (1818–83). Capital, volume I (1867).
- Labour power is a commodity; surplus value arises because workers produce more value than their wage.
- Capitalists accumulate; competition drives mechanisation, which Marx believed would tend to lower the rate of profit.
- A "reserve army of labour" restrains wages; crises and class conflict would eventually transform the system.
- Historical materialism: economic base shapes the institutional superstructure.

Applied illustration (comparative advantage). If Portugal needs 80 labour units for wine and 90 for cloth while England needs 120 and 100, Portugal's opportunity cost of wine is 80/90 ≈ 0.89 cloth versus England's 1.2, so Portugal should specialise in wine and England in cloth.

Exam pitfalls
- Reducing Smith to laissez-faire.
- Confusing comparative and absolute advantage.
- Treating Marx as a mere critic: he built on Ricardian value theory.

notes.h: Keynes, Hayek and modern schools of thought
notes.body:
J. M. Keynes (1883–1946). The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money (1936) argued that market economies can settle at equilibrium with involuntary unemployment because of deficient effective demand.
- Rejected Say's law; output is determined by aggregate demand.
- Saving and investment are reconciled by changes in income, not the interest rate; the multiplier amplifies changes in investment.
- Interest is a reward for parting with liquidity (liquidity preference); in a slump, monetary policy may be weak.
- Investment depends on uncertain expectations and "animal spirits". Money wage cuts may not restore employment because they reduce demand and raise real debt burdens.
- Policy: public works and active management of demand.

F. A. Hayek (1899–1992). In 1930s debates Hayek's Austrian business-cycle theory blamed booms on credit expansion that pushed interest rates below the natural rate, distorting the structure of production; the slump was the necessary liquidation of malinvestment. In "The Use of Knowledge in Society" (1945) he argued prices aggregate dispersed knowledge that no planner could gather, a key argument in the socialist calculation debate (with Mises against Lange). The Road to Serfdom (1944) warned that central planning threatened liberty.

The neoclassical synthesis. Hicks (1937) and Samuelson combined Keynesian short-run analysis (IS–LM) with neoclassical long-run equilibrium, dominating the 1950s–60s.

Monetarism. Friedman revived the quantity theory (MV = PY), argued "inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon", attacked the stable Phillips curve (1968) and favoured rules such as constant money growth.

New classical macroeconomics. Lucas, Sargent and Prescott introduced rational expectations. The Lucas critique (1976) argued that parameters estimated under one policy regime change when policy changes. Real business cycle theory (Kydland and Prescott, 1982) modelled fluctuations as efficient responses to technology shocks.

New Keynesian economics. Mankiw, Akerlof, Yellen, Blanchard and others built rational-expectations models with sticky prices and wages (menu costs, staggered contracts), leading to the DSGE "new synthesis" used by central banks.

Post-Keynesians (Robinson, Kalecki, Minsky) stress fundamental uncertainty, distribution and financial instability; Modern Monetary Theory is a recent offshoot. The 2008 crisis revived interest in Minsky and in finance-macro links.

Applied illustration. Faced with a 1930s-style slump, Keynes would advise loan-financed public works; Hayek (at the time) warned that credit expansion would merely postpone necessary adjustment.

Exam pitfalls
- Equating Keynes with permanent deficits: he favoured balanced current budgets with variable capital spending.
- Treating "Keynesian" and "New Keynesian" as identical.
- Reducing Hayek to anti-state polemic: his knowledge argument is analytical.

cards.f: What is the Malthusian trap?
cards.b: A pre-industrial equilibrium in which higher income raises population growth until wages fall back to subsistence, so technical progress raises population density rather than living standards.

cards.f: Who coined the term 'Great Divergence' and in which book?
cards.b: Kenneth Pomeranz, in The Great Divergence (2000).

cards.f: What was Pomeranz's central claim?
cards.b: That core regions such as the Yangzi delta and England were broadly comparable around 1750, and that Britain pulled ahead thanks largely to accessible coal and New World resources ('ghost acres').

cards.f: What is the 'Little Divergence'?
cards.b: The pulling ahead of the North Sea economies (England and the Low Countries) from southern and central Europe in real wages and income from the 16th–17th centuries.

cards.f: How did the Black Death affect real wages in western Europe?
cards.b: By sharply reducing population, it raised the land–labour ratio and real wages rose substantially over the following century, as Malthusian logic predicts.

cards.f: What is de Vries's 'industrious revolution'?
cards.b: The idea that from the 17th century households reallocated time towards market work, working harder to buy new consumer goods, raising output before mechanisation.

cards.f: What is Smithian growth?
cards.b: Growth from specialisation and the extension of markets, as opposed to growth based on sustained technological innovation.

cards.f: How do Broadberry and co-authors challenge the California School?
cards.b: Their GDP reconstructions suggest China's income per head fell behind England and Holland well before 1750, pushing the divergence earlier.

cards.f: What institutional explanation do North and Weingast (1989) offer?
cards.b: The Glorious Revolution of 1688 constrained the Crown, made state commitments credible and secured property rights, enabling public and private finance to develop.

cards.f: What is Mokyr's 'culture of growth' argument?
cards.b: That a European intellectual culture, notably the Republic of Letters, valued useful knowledge and fostered competition in ideas, preparing the ground for sustained innovation.

cards.f: Approximately when is the British Industrial Revolution usually dated?
cards.b: Roughly 1760 to 1830–40.

cards.f: What did Watt's separate condenser achieve?
cards.b: Patented in 1769, it greatly improved the fuel efficiency of steam engines compared with Newcomen's design by avoiding repeated cooling of the cylinder.

cards.f: What did the Crafts–Harley revision show?
cards.b: That aggregate growth in output per head during the Industrial Revolution was slow, well under 1% a year before 1830, because modern sectors were small; change was structural rather than a sudden take-off.

cards.f: State Allen's high-wage, cheap-energy hypothesis.
cards.b: Britain's high wages and cheap coal made labour-saving, energy-intensive machinery profitable there first, explaining why the key inventions were British (Allen, 2009).

cards.f: What is Mokyr's 'Industrial Enlightenment'?
cards.b: The links forged between scientific inquiry and practical artisans in 18th-century Britain and Europe, which expanded and spread useful knowledge feeding invention.

cards.f: What is 'Engels' pause'?
cards.b: Allen's term for the period (to about the 1840s) when output per worker rose but real wages stagnated, so the profit share increased.

cards.f: When did steam overtake water power in British industry?
cards.b: Only around the 1830s; water remained the main source of mechanical power in early factories.

cards.f: Who invented the water frame and what was its significance?
cards.b: Richard Arkwright (patented 1769); powered by water, it produced strong yarn and helped establish the factory system, notably at Cromford.

cards.f: What did Feinstein (1998) find on living standards?
cards.b: That real wages rose only slowly between the 1770s and 1830s, supporting a cautious view of early gains for workers.

cards.f: What is Wrigley's distinction between organic and mineral economies?
cards.b: Organic economies are limited by land producing food, fuel and raw materials; using coal freed Britain from this energy constraint.

cards.f: What drove commodity price convergence in 1870–1914?
cards.b: Falling transport costs (steamships, railways, the Suez Canal) and the telegraph, which integrated markets for goods such as wheat.

cards.f: What did O'Rourke and Williamson argue in Globalization and History (1999)?
cards.b: That 19th-century integration caused commodity price and factor price convergence, with distributional effects that generated a political backlash.

cards.f: How did cheap New World grain affect European landowners and workers?
cards.b: Landowners lost as rents fell; workers gained from cheaper food, consistent with Heckscher–Ohlin predictions.

cards.f: Name two continental responses to the grain invasion.
cards.b: Germany's 1879 tariff under Bismarck and France's Méline tariff (1892). Britain maintained free trade.

cards.f: Explain Hume's price-specie-flow mechanism.
cards.b: A deficit country loses gold, its money supply and prices fall, its goods become more competitive, and the deficit corrects (Hume, 1752).

cards.f: What were the 'rules of the game'?
cards.b: The expectation that central banks would reinforce gold flows, raising rates when losing gold; in practice they often sterilised flows.

cards.f: Why was the classical gold standard credible according to Eichengreen?
cards.b: Commitment to convertibility was rarely doubted, partly because limited suffrage and weak labour movements reduced pressure to prioritise employment, and central banks cooperated in crises.

cards.f: In trilemma terms, what did the gold standard choose?
cards.b: Fixed exchange rates and free capital mobility, sacrificing independent monetary policy.

cards.f: What was the Baring crisis?
cards.b: In 1890 Barings faced collapse over Argentine bond exposure; the Bank of England organised a rescue, illustrating periphery fragility and London's crisis management.

cards.f: What role did the Bank of England's Bank Rate play under gold?
cards.b: Raising Bank Rate drew short-term capital into London quickly, defending sterling with remarkably small gold reserves.

cards.f: At what parity did Britain return to gold in 1925?
cards.b: The prewar rate of $4.86, a decision by Chancellor Churchill that Keynes argued overvalued sterling.

cards.f: What did Friedman and Schwartz (1963) argue caused the Great Depression?
cards.b: The Fed's failure to stop the money stock falling by about a third, amid waves of bank failures, turned a recession into a depression.

cards.f: What was Bernanke's (1983) non-monetary channel?
cards.b: Bank failures destroyed information and relationships needed for credit intermediation, cutting lending beyond the effect of the fall in money.

cards.f: What did Eichengreen and Sachs (1985) find?
cards.b: Countries that left the gold standard or devalued earlier recovered earlier, because they could expand money and escape deflation.

cards.f: When did Britain leave gold, and when did the Gold Bloc collapse?
cards.b: Britain left in September 1931; the Gold Bloc, led by France, held out until 1936.

cards.f: What was the Smoot–Hawley tariff and how important was it?
cards.b: A 1930 US tariff increase that prompted retaliation and contributed to the trade collapse, but most economists see it as secondary to monetary causes.

cards.f: Name two 1933 US banking reforms.
cards.b: The Glass–Steagall (Banking) Act separating commercial and investment banking, and federal deposit insurance via the FDIC.

cards.f: What was the 1937–38 'recession within the depression'?
cards.b: A sharp US downturn after monetary tightening (higher reserve requirements, gold sterilisation) and fiscal consolidation.

cards.f: Why was the interwar gold-exchange standard fragile?
cards.b: Scarce and maldistributed reserves (France and the US sterilised gold), misaligned parities, weak central bank cooperation, and democratic pressure making deflation costly.

cards.f: What was Sweden's monetary policy innovation in 1931?
cards.b: After leaving gold it announced a price-level stabilisation objective, an early forerunner of inflation targeting.

cards.f: What were the key features of the Bretton Woods system?
cards.b: Currencies pegged to the dollar, the dollar convertible to gold at $35 an ounce for official holders, adjustable pegs and permitted capital controls, overseen by the IMF.

cards.f: What is Triffin's dilemma?
cards.b: The world needed growing dollar reserves, but rising US liabilities relative to gold undermined confidence in convertibility.

cards.f: When did Nixon close the gold window?
cards.b: August 1971; generalised floating followed in 1973.

cards.f: Why did Europe grow so fast in 1950–73 according to catch-up theory?
cards.b: It was far behind the US frontier and could adopt existing technology rapidly, given sufficient 'social capability' (Abramovitz, 1986).

cards.f: What was the European Payments Union?
cards.b: A 1950 multilateral clearing arrangement that allowed European trade to expand before full currency convertibility, restored in 1958.

cards.f: What did DeLong and Eichengreen argue about Marshall Aid?
cards.b: That its main contribution was not the money itself but supporting stabilisation and market-oriented policies, a 'structural adjustment programme'.

cards.f: What is Gerschenkron's 'relative backwardness'?
cards.b: Late developers can grow faster and use substitutes such as banks or the state to overcome missing prerequisites.

cards.f: Give three explanations for Britain's slower postwar growth.
cards.b: Less scope for catch-up, stop–go policy under balance-of-payments constraints, and weak industrial relations or management (also late EEC entry).

cards.f: When was sterling devalued in the Bretton Woods era?
How did structural change contribute to golden age growth?
cards.b: Labour moved from low-productivity agriculture to higher-productivity industry and services, raising aggregate productivity.

cards.f: What were the two oil shocks of the 1970s?
cards.b: 1973–74 (OPEC embargo) and 1979–80 (Iranian Revolution), both contributing to stagflation.

cards.f: What triggered the Latin American debt crisis?
cards.b: Mexico's 1982 moratorium after US interest rates rose sharply, making floating-rate petrodollar loans unpayable.

cards.f: What was Black Wednesday?
cards.b: 16 September 1992, when sterling left the ERM after speculative attack; the UK adopted inflation targeting in October 1992.

cards.f: Why is the ERM crisis a second-generation crisis?
cards.b: Fundamentals were not unsustainable, but high German rates made defending the peg costly, so markets bet the government would choose to abandon it.

cards.f: What were the main causes of the 1997 Asian financial crisis?
cards.b: Short-term foreign-currency borrowing, pegged exchange rates, weak bank regulation and asset bubbles, followed by contagion after Thailand floated the baht in July 1997.

cards.f: What criticism did Stiglitz make of the IMF in Asia?
cards.b: That demanding fiscal austerity and high interest rates in a private-sector crisis deepened recessions, and that rapid capital-account liberalisation had been premature.

cards.f: What was the Washington Consensus?
cards.b: John Williamson's 1989 summary of reforms promoted for developing countries: fiscal discipline, liberalisation of trade and finance, privatisation and deregulation.

cards.f: State Rodrik's globalisation trilemma.
cards.b: Deep economic integration, national sovereignty and democratic politics cannot all be fully achieved at once.

cards.f: When was the WTO established and when did China join?
cards.b: The WTO was created in 1995 after the Uruguay Round; China joined in 2001.

cards.f: What was the Brady Plan?
cards.b: A 1989 US-led scheme that converted Latin American bank loans into tradable bonds with partial debt reduction, ending the debt crisis.

cards.f: What does Smith's pin factory illustrate?
cards.b: That the division of labour vastly increases productivity through dexterity, saved time and specialised machinery, limited by the extent of the market.

cards.f: What is the context of Smith's 'invisible hand' in the Wealth of Nations?
cards.b: It appears once, describing how a merchant preferring domestic investment for his own security unintentionally promotes the public interest.

cards.f: Name three roles Smith assigned to the state.
cards.b: Defence, the administration of justice, and public works and institutions such as roads and education.

cards.f: Define comparative advantage.
cards.b: A country has comparative advantage in a good if it can produce it at lower opportunity cost than another country; trade on this basis benefits both (Ricardo, 1817).

cards.f: Explain Ricardo's theory of differential rent.
cards.b: As cultivation extends to less fertile land, the better land earns a rent equal to its productivity advantage; rising population raises rents and squeezes profits.

cards.f: Why did Ricardo oppose the Corn Laws?
cards.b: They raised grain prices and rents, reduced profits and capital accumulation, and pushed the economy towards a stationary state.

cards.f: Distinguish Malthus's positive and preventive checks.
cards.b: Positive checks raise mortality (famine, disease, war); preventive checks lower births (delayed marriage, moral restraint).

cards.f: On what did Malthus disagree with Ricardo about gluts?
cards.b: Malthus argued general gluts from insufficient effective demand were possible; Ricardo, following Say, denied this.

cards.f: What is surplus value in Marx?
cards.b: The difference between the value workers produce and the value of their labour power (the wage), appropriated by capitalists as profit.

cards.f: What is Marx's 'reserve army of labour'?
cards.b: The unemployed and underemployed whose presence restrains wages; mechanisation tends to replenish it.

cards.f: What is effective demand in Keynes's General Theory?
cards.b: Aggregate spending that determines output and employment; if it is deficient, the economy can rest at equilibrium with involuntary unemployment.

cards.f: What is liquidity preference?
cards.b: Keynes's theory that the interest rate is the reward for parting with liquidity, determined by money demand and supply rather than saving and investment.

cards.f: Why did Keynes doubt that money wage cuts would cure unemployment?
cards.b: Cuts reduce workers' incomes and demand, raise real debt burdens and may cause expectations of further falls, so employment may not recover.

cards.f: Summarise Austrian business-cycle theory.
cards.b: Credit expansion pushes interest rates below the natural rate, causing malinvestment in long production processes; the bust is the liquidation of these errors (Mises, Hayek).

cards.f: What is the core argument of Hayek's 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' (1945)?
cards.b: Economic knowledge is dispersed and local; prices coordinate it in ways no central planner could replicate.

cards.f: What was the neoclassical synthesis?
cards.b: The postwar combination of Keynesian short-run analysis (IS–LM) with neoclassical long-run equilibrium, associated with Hicks and Samuelson.

cards.f: State the Lucas critique.
cards.b: Relationships estimated under one policy regime may change when policy changes, because agents' expectations and decisions depend on the policy rule (Lucas, 1976).

cards.f: What is real business cycle theory?
cards.b: Kydland and Prescott's (1982) view that fluctuations are efficient responses of rational agents to real shocks, mainly technology, implying little role for stabilisation policy.

cards.f: How does New Keynesian economics differ from new classical economics?
cards.b: It keeps rational expectations and microfoundations but adds nominal rigidities and imperfect competition, so monetary policy has real short-run effects.

cards.f: Name three Post-Keynesian thinkers and a shared theme.
cards.b: Joan Robinson, Michał Kalecki and Hyman Minsky; they emphasise fundamental uncertainty, distribution and financial instability.

questions.q: In a Malthusian economy, a permanent improvement in agricultural technology leads in the long run to:
options: permanently higher real wages
a larger population at roughly the same living standard
a smaller population with higher wages
sustained growth in income per head
questions.why: Higher income raises population growth until wages return to subsistence, so technology raises population density rather than living standards.

questions.q: Which statement best represents Pomeranz's argument in The Great Divergence (2000)?
options: China was poorer than Europe from the Middle Ages because of despotic institutions
Core regions of China and Europe were broadly similar until about 1750, and Britain's lead owed much to coal and New World resources
Europe's lead arose from superior Protestant culture in the 16th century
The divergence was caused mainly by the Opium Wars
questions.why: Pomeranz stressed comparability of core regions such as the Yangzi delta and England until the late 18th century, and the role of coal and colonial 'ghost acres'.

questions.q: The Crafts–Harley revision of the Industrial Revolution argued that:
options: aggregate growth was rapid from the 1760s, at over 3% per head a year
aggregate growth in output per head was slow before 1830 even though structural change was dramatic
the Industrial Revolution did not involve technical change
Britain industrialised later than France
questions.why: Their estimates showed modest growth in output per head because modern sectors were small, while the economy's structure changed profoundly.

questions.q: Under the classical gold standard, a country could not simultaneously maintain fixed exchange rates, free capital flows and:
options: free trade
an independent monetary policy
a current account surplus
a central bank
questions.why: This is the trilemma: the gold standard combined fixed rates and capital mobility, so monetary policy had to defend convertibility.

questions.q: Which country, among the following, left the gold standard first in the 1930s and therefore, on Eichengreen and Sachs's argument, recovered relatively early?
options: France
The United Kingdom
Belgium
Switzerland
questions.why: Britain left gold in September 1931; France, Belgium and Switzerland were Gold Bloc members that held on until 1935–36.

questions.q: Under the Bretton Woods system, the US dollar was convertible into gold for official holders at:
options: $20.67 an ounce
$35 an ounce
$42.22 an ounce
$4.86 an ounce
questions.why: The $35 official price was set in 1934 and anchored Bretton Woods. $20.67 was the pre-1933 price; $4.86 was the sterling–dollar parity.

questions.q: The 1992 ERM crisis is usually classified as a 'second-generation' currency crisis because:
options: the UK was monetising large fiscal deficits
defending the peg required interest rates that were politically costly, so a speculative attack could succeed even without unsustainable fundamentals
banks had large unhedged dollar debts
the UK had a hard currency board
questions.why: Second-generation models (Obstfeld, 1994) feature governments weighing the costs of defence; high German rates after reunification made defence costly in a weak UK economy.

questions.q: Portugal needs 80 labour units to produce a unit of wine and 90 for cloth; England needs 120 for wine and 100 for cloth. Under Ricardian comparative advantage:
options: Portugal should produce both goods
England should specialise in wine and Portugal in cloth
Portugal should specialise in wine and England in cloth
No gains from trade exist because Portugal has absolute advantage in both
questions.why: Portugal's opportunity cost of wine is 80/90 ≈ 0.89 cloth, England's 120/100 = 1.2, so Portugal has comparative advantage in wine and England in cloth.

questions.q: The Lucas critique (1976) states that:
options: markets always clear instantly
parameters of macroeconometric models estimated under one policy regime may shift when the policy regime changes
money is neutral in the short and long run
fiscal policy has no effect on output
questions.why: Because agents' decisions depend on expected policy, reduced-form relationships such as the Phillips curve are not invariant to policy changes.

questions.q: Which of the following positions is most clearly associated with Hayek rather than Keynes in the 1930s debates?
options: Saving and investment are equated by changes in income
A slump reflects the liquidation of malinvestment caused by an earlier credit expansion that pushed interest rates below the natural rate
Public works financed by borrowing can raise employment in a slump
Liquidity preference determines the interest rate
questions.why: Hayek's Austrian theory traced the bust to credit-induced distortions in the structure of production; the other options are Keynesian.

questions.q: Explain why real wages in England rose after the Black Death, using the Malthusian model.
markScheme: Plague cut population sharply (perhaps a third or more)
Land–labour ratio rose, raising marginal product of labour and real wages
Malthusian prediction: higher wages eventually raise population again, though in England wages stayed relatively high for a long period
questions.modelAnswer: The Black Death of 1347–51 killed a large share of England's population, perhaps a third or more. With land unchanged, each worker had more land to work, so the marginal product of labour and real wages rose; landlords faced labour shortages despite attempts to cap wages such as the Statute of Labourers (1351). In the Malthusian model, higher living standards should eventually raise population and push wages back down. Recurrent plague kept population low, and wages remained high for over a century.

questions.q: Compare Allen's and Mokyr's explanations of why the Industrial Revolution began in Britain.
markScheme: Allen: demand-side/incentive explanation — high wages relative to capital and cheap coal made labour-saving, energy-intensive machinery profitable in Britain
Allen's evidence: wage and price comparisons across Europe and Asia
Mokyr: supply-side — Industrial Enlightenment and culture of useful knowledge linking science and craft
Mokyr emphasises skilled artisans and diffusion of knowledge, not just factor prices
Evaluation: complementary (incentives to invent plus capacity to invent); critiques e.g. Humphries/Schneider on wages, difficulty measuring culture
questions.modelAnswer: Allen (2009) offers an incentive-based explanation: by 1700 British wages were high relative to the price of capital and energy, while coal was cheap. Machines such as the spinning jenny and steam engine saved labour and used energy, so they were profitable to develop in Britain but not in low-wage France or India. Mokyr instead emphasises the supply of invention: an Industrial Enlightenment connected scientific knowledge with skilled artisans and engineers, creating a culture that sought to apply useful knowledge. Factor prices explain why inventors focused on particular techniques; knowledge explains why inventions kept coming after initial breakthroughs. They are complementary, though Allen's wage data have been challenged and Mokyr's cultural factors are hard to measure.

questions.q: Explain how the classical gold standard adjusted to a balance-of-payments deficit, distinguishing theory from practice.
markScheme: Theory: Hume's price-specie-flow mechanism — gold outflow, money supply falls, prices fall, competitiveness improves
Practice: central banks raised discount rates, attracting short-term capital quickly
Rules of the game often broken via sterilisation
Credibility meant stabilising capital flows; adjustment burden fell harder on periphery
questions.modelAnswer: In Hume's price-specie-flow mechanism, a deficit country loses gold, its money supply contracts, prices fall and its goods become cheaper, so exports rise and imports fall until balance returns. In practice adjustment worked mostly through capital flows. The Bank of England raised Bank Rate when gold flowed out, drawing short-term funds into London within days. Central banks often sterilised flows rather than following the 'rules of the game'. Because markets trusted that parities would be maintained, speculation tended to stabilise currencies. Periphery economies, lacking this credibility, faced harsher adjustment and more crises.

questions.q: Assess the role of the gold standard in causing and spreading the Great Depression.
markScheme: Gold standard transmitted US monetary contraction internationally (fixed rates)
Asymmetric adjustment: deficit countries forced to deflate, surplus countries (US, France) sterilised gold
Defence of parities required tight money amid banking crises (e.g. Fed raising rates in October 1931)
Evidence: earlier leavers recovered sooner (Eichengreen and Sachs 1985)
Balance: domestic factors also mattered (bank failures, Fed policy errors, debt deflation)
questions.modelAnswer: The gold-exchange standard linked countries' money supplies, so the US and French accumulation of gold in 1928–30 forced deflation elsewhere. Adjustment was asymmetric: deficit countries had to contract while surplus countries sterilised inflows. Commitment to gold also stopped central banks acting as lenders of last resort; after Britain left in 1931, the Fed raised rates to defend the dollar despite banking panics. Eichengreen and Sachs (1985) showed that countries leaving gold earlier recovered sooner. Yet domestic failures mattered too: the Fed's passivity during bank runs, debt deflation and the collapse of confidence. The gold standard is best seen as the transmission mechanism and constraint that made national slumps global.

questions.q: Explain Triffin's dilemma and how it contributed to the collapse of Bretton Woods.
markScheme: World trade growth required more dollar reserves, supplied through US deficits
Growing dollar liabilities relative to US gold stock undermined confidence in convertibility at $35
Combined with US inflation and Vietnam spending, pressure built (gold pool collapse 1968)
Nixon closed the gold window in August 1971; generalised floating by 1973
questions.modelAnswer: Triffin (1960) noted that the Bretton Woods system relied on the dollar as the main reserve asset. To supply liquidity for expanding world trade, the US had to run balance-of-payments deficits, but as foreign official dollar holdings grew relative to US gold reserves, confidence that dollars could be converted at $35 an ounce eroded. US inflation in the late 1960s, linked to Vietnam war spending and expansionary policy, worsened the imbalance. The London Gold Pool broke down in 1968, and Nixon suspended convertibility in August 1971; after the Smithsonian realignment failed, major currencies floated from 1973.

questions.q: Why did the 1997 Asian financial crisis spread from Thailand to economies such as Korea and Indonesia?
markScheme: Common vulnerabilities: short-term foreign-currency debt, pegged exchange rates, weak bank supervision
Balance-sheet effects: depreciation raised local-currency value of debts, causing defaults
Investor reassessment/herding and common lender withdrawal (wake-up call contagion)
Policy responses (IMF austerity, high rates) arguably deepened slumps
questions.modelAnswer: Contagion reflected shared weaknesses and investor behaviour. Many Asian economies had pegged or tightly managed exchange rates and had borrowed heavily in short-term dollars, often through lightly regulated banks. When Thailand floated the baht in July 1997, investors reassessed similar economies and withdrew funds, a 'wake-up call'. Depreciation then raised the local-currency value of foreign debts, causing corporate and bank failures that weakened economies further. Common creditors, such as Japanese and European banks, cut lending across the region. IMF programmes demanding high interest rates and fiscal tightening may have deepened the downturns.

questions.q: Outline Malthus's principle of population.
markScheme: Population tends to grow geometrically, subsistence arithmetically
Positive checks (higher mortality: famine, disease, war)
Preventive checks (lower fertility: delayed marriage, moral restraint)
questions.modelAnswer: In An Essay on the Principle of Population (1798), Malthus argued that unchecked population tends to grow geometrically, whereas food supply grows at best arithmetically. Population therefore presses against the means of subsistence. It is held in check by positive checks, which raise mortality, such as famine, disease and war, and by preventive checks, which lower fertility, such as later marriage and what he later called moral restraint. As a result, living standards for most people tend to remain close to subsistence.

questions.q: Is it fair to describe Adam Smith as an advocate of laissez-faire?
markScheme: Smith attacked mercantilism and favoured 'natural liberty' and free trade
Invisible hand: self-interest can serve the public good in competitive markets
But assigned state roles: defence, justice, public works, education
Distrust of merchants' collusion; supported some regulation (e.g. Navigation Acts for defence, usury ceilings)
Moral Sentiments: markets embedded in moral and social norms; conclusion: qualified liberal, not dogmatic laissez-faire
questions.modelAnswer: Smith attacked mercantilist restrictions and argued that a system of natural liberty would raise national wealth; his invisible hand passage suggests self-interest can promote the public good. But he was no doctrinaire. The sovereign had three duties: defence, the administration of justice, and certain public works and institutions, including roads and elementary education to counter the stultifying effects of the division of labour. He warned that merchants conspire against the public, supported the Navigation Acts for defence and favoured a legal ceiling on interest rates. The Theory of Moral Sentiments shows that he saw markets as embedded in moral norms. 'Laissez-faire' is a later label; Smith is better described as a pragmatic liberal.

questions.q: Explain how Keynes's General Theory challenged classical economics.
markScheme: Rejected Say's law: supply does not create its own demand
Output and employment determined by effective demand; equilibrium with involuntary unemployment possible
Saving and investment equated by income changes (multiplier), not the interest rate
Interest determined by liquidity preference; wage cuts not a reliable cure; policy implication: demand management/public works
questions.modelAnswer: Classical economists held that flexible wages and interest rates would restore full employment, and that Say's law ruled out general gluts. Keynes argued that output is determined by effective demand and that the economy can settle at an equilibrium with involuntary unemployment. If investment falls, income falls via the multiplier until saving matches the lower investment: income, not the interest rate, does the equilibrating. The interest rate reflects liquidity preference, so it may not fall enough. Money wage cuts reduce demand and raise real debts, so they may not restore employment. The policy implication was active demand management, including public works.

questions.q: Compare monetarism with New Keynesian economics on the effectiveness of monetary policy.
markScheme: Monetarism (Friedman): money matters for nominal income; long-run neutrality; vertical long-run Phillips curve
Monetarists favoured rules (constant money growth) because of long and variable lags and policy error
New Keynesians: nominal rigidities give monetary policy short-run real effects even with rational expectations
New Keynesians favour interest-rate rules / inflation targeting; differences over instruments (money vs rates) and activism
questions.modelAnswer: Monetarists, led by Friedman, held that changes in the money supply drive nominal income, that money is neutral in the long run and that the long-run Phillips curve is vertical. Because policy acts with long and variable lags, they distrusted discretion and favoured a fixed money-growth rule. New Keynesians share long-run neutrality but build in sticky prices and wages, so even with rational expectations monetary policy has substantial short-run real effects and can stabilise demand shocks. They model policy as an interest-rate rule, such as inflation targeting, rather than money growth, since money demand proved unstable in the 1980s.

questions.q: 'The Great Divergence happened in the eighteenth century and was an accident of geography.' Discuss.
markScheme: Sets out Pomeranz/California School: comparable core regions c.1750; coal and New World 'ghost acres'
Timing debate: Broadberry et al. GDP estimates and Allen wage data suggest earlier divergence (17th century or before)
Little Divergence within Europe indicates North Sea dynamism predating coal-based industry
Geography: coal location near markets/water transport; Atlantic access
Institutional alternatives: North and Weingast; AJR Atlantic trade and merchant power
Cultural/ideas explanations: Mokyr's culture of growth, McCloskey
Factor prices: Allen's high-wage economy, itself partly a product of earlier commercial success
State fragmentation and competition in Europe
Assessment: geography as necessary but not sufficient; interaction of factors
Clear, reasoned conclusion on timing and causation
questions.modelAnswer:
The proposition combines a claim about timing with a claim about causation, both drawn from Pomeranz's Great Divergence (2000). Pomeranz argued that the Yangzi delta and England were broadly comparable in living standards, market development and ecological pressure around 1750. Britain escaped because its coal lay close to markets and water transport, and because New World land and slavery supplied cotton, sugar and timber, the 'ghost acres' that relieved land constraints.

On timing, newer quantitative work is sceptical. Broadberry and co-authors reconstruct GDP per head showing China falling behind England and Holland from the 17th century or earlier, and Allen's real-wage comparisons place Yangzi delta labourers below their London counterparts well before 1800. The Little Divergence within Europe, in which London and Amsterdam pulled away from southern Europe, also indicates that North Sea dynamism predated coal-fired industry.

On causation, geography clearly mattered. Wrigley's account of the shift from an organic to a mineral economy shows how coal broke an energy constraint. But calling it an 'accident' understates human agency. Institutional accounts stress constraints on the Crown after 1688 (North and Weingast, 1989) and the way Atlantic trade strengthened merchant interests (Acemoglu, Johnson and Robinson, 2005). Mokyr points to a European culture of useful knowledge, and to competition between fragmented states that limited the suppression of new ideas. Allen's high-wage economy, which made labour-saving technology profitable, was itself a product of earlier commercial success.

Even colonial resources were not an accident: they required naval power, financial institutions and coercion.

A balanced conclusion is that the divergence in income began earlier than 1750 in north-western Europe, while the divergence in growth rates, driven by industrialisation, took off after 1800. Geography helped decide where and how industrialisation happened, but institutions, ideas and earlier commercial growth explain why north-western Europe was positioned to exploit it.

questions.q: 'The Industrial Revolution was neither industrial nor a revolution.' Evaluate this claim with reference to recent quantitative research.
markScheme: Explains the claim: slow aggregate growth (Crafts–Harley) and limited spread of factory industry
Evidence: output per head growth under 1% a year before 1830; modest TFP growth
Much growth in traditional sectors and services; agriculture's productivity gains
Counter: structural change — falling agricultural employment share, urbanisation
Sectoral transformation in cotton, iron, steam; productivity gains of orders of magnitude in spinning
Long-run discontinuity: break from Malthusian regime to sustained growth
Steam's slow diffusion (1830s); general purpose technology lags
Living standards debate (Feinstein, Allen's Engels' pause)
Conclusion: revolution in trajectory, not speed
questions.modelAnswer:
The claim reflects revisionist research in the 1980s. Crafts and Harley re-estimated British growth and found that output per head grew well under 1% a year before 1830, far slower than older estimates or Rostow's dramatic take-off implied. Productivity growth was modest, and much economic activity continued in small workshops, agriculture and services. In this sense the change was neither sudden nor confined to factory industry.

Yet the claim goes too far. First, the economy's structure was transformed. The share of the labour force in agriculture fell sharply, and Britain became the most urbanised and industrialised society in the world. Second, specific sectors were revolutionised. In cotton spinning, labour required per unit of yarn fell by orders of magnitude between hand methods and powered mules, and yarn prices collapsed. Iron production was transformed by coke smelting and Cort's puddling process. Slow aggregate growth reflects simple arithmetic: modern sectors were initially a small share of output, so even spectacular growth within them only gradually raised the national average.

Third, the significance of the Industrial Revolution lies in its trajectory. Growth rates rose from near zero to sustained growth that never reverted, ending the Malthusian regime. General purpose technologies such as steam took decades to diffuse: steam overtook water power only in the 1830s, and railways came later still, so the biggest productivity effects lay after 1830.

Living standards also rose slowly: Feinstein's real-wage series and Allen's 'Engels' pause' show workers gained little before the 1840s, which reinforces the image of an uneven, gradual process.

The best conclusion is that the Industrial Revolution was revolutionary in its long-run consequences and in its structural change, but evolutionary in its pace. 'Industrious' as well as industrial changes mattered, but the decisive break with the past justifies the label.

questions.q: 'The success of the classical gold standard, 1870–1914, owed more to the political and economic circumstances of the period than to any automatic mechanism.' Discuss.
markScheme: Describes the mechanism: Hume price-specie-flow; fixed parities; gold points
Evidence that the automatic mechanism was weak: sterilisation, violations of rules of the game (Bloomfield)
Capital flows and Bank Rate as main adjustment tool; London centrality
Credibility: stabilising speculation; commitment rarely questioned
Political circumstances: limited franchise, weak unions, low priority on employment (Eichengreen)
International cooperation in crises (e.g. Baring 1890, help from Banque de France)
Favourable conditions: growing gold supply after 1890s discoveries; peace; expanding trade and capital exports
Limits of success: periphery crises, deflation 1873–96, bank panics in the US
Contrast with interwar failure when circumstances changed
Conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
The classical gold standard is often remembered as a self-regulating system. In Hume's price-specie-flow mechanism, a deficit country lost gold, its prices fell and its competitiveness recovered. Yet the historical evidence suggests that this mechanism did little of the work.

First, central banks often broke the 'rules of the game'. Bloomfield's research found that they frequently sterilised gold flows rather than allowing them to change domestic money supplies. Adjustment worked mainly through capital flows: a rise in Bank Rate drew short-term funds into London within days, so the Bank of England defended sterling with small reserves.

Second, this worked because the system was credible. Markets believed that core countries would maintain convertibility, so when a currency weakened, speculators bought it, expecting recovery. Eichengreen (Golden Fetters, 1992) argues credibility rested on political conditions: limited suffrage and weak labour movements meant governments faced little pressure to prioritise employment over the exchange rate.

Third, cooperation underpinned stability. In the Baring crisis of 1890, the Bank of England borrowed gold from the Banque de France and the Russian state bank. London's centrality and Britain's role as a capital exporter recycled funds.

Favourable economic conditions also helped. The period was largely peaceful, trade was expanding, and gold discoveries in South Africa and elsewhere from the 1890s eased the deflation of 1873–96.

The system was not an unqualified success. Periphery economies such as Argentina suffered crises, and the US experienced severe banking panics, notably in 1907. The interwar failure is telling: once suffrage widened, unions strengthened, reserves became maldistributed and cooperation weakened, the restored standard collapsed within six years.

The proposition is therefore largely persuasive. The gold standard's mechanics mattered less than the credibility, cooperation and political economy that supported it; it was a social and political institution as much as a monetary one.

questions.q:
In 1929, the fictional nation of Westmark has a fixed gold parity, a fragile banking system and large debts owed by farmers. Over 1930–32 its central bank raises interest rates twice to stem gold outflows; 30% of its banks fail; prices fall by 25%; and unemployment rises from 4% to 22%. Its neighbour Eastland left gold in late 1931, devalued by 30% and cut interest rates; its prices stabilised in 1932 and industrial production began to recover in 1933.

Using economic theory and historical evidence from the Great Depression, explain the contrasting experiences of Westmark and Eastland.
markScheme: Westmark's tightening to defend gold: golden fetters / trilemma constraint
Monetary contraction via bank failures (money multiplier collapse), as in Friedman–Schwartz
Credit channel: loss of bank lending relationships (Bernanke 1983)
Debt deflation: 25% fall in prices raises real farm debt burdens, distress sales (Fisher 1933)
Real interest rates very high with falling prices
Eastland: leaving gold freed monetary policy; devaluation boosted competitiveness and ended deflation expectations
Evidence: Eichengreen and Sachs (1985) — earlier leavers recovered sooner; examples UK 1931, Sweden, vs Gold Bloc (France)
Beggar-thy-neighbour concern versus net global benefit from monetary expansion
Conclusion linking Westmark to Gold Bloc / US 1931–33 experience
questions.modelAnswer:
Westmark's experience mirrors that of the United States in 1930–33 and of the Gold Bloc. Its commitment to a fixed gold parity meant that when gold flowed out, the central bank raised rates rather than easing, the trap Eichengreen calls the 'golden fetters'. In trilemma terms, with fixed rates and capital mobility, monetary policy could not respond to the domestic slump. The Fed did the same in October 1931 after Britain left gold.

Bank failures amplified the contraction. Friedman and Schwartz (1963) showed that as depositors withdrew cash and banks hoarded reserves, the money multiplier collapsed and the US money stock fell by about a third. Bernanke (1983) added a credit channel: when banks failed, borrowers lost lending relationships that could not be quickly replaced, so credit to farms and small firms dried up.

Falling prices made matters worse. With prices down 25%, the real burden of Westmark's farm debts rose by about a third (1/0.75 ≈ 1.33). Fisher's (1933) debt deflation predicts distress sales, further falls in prices and more defaults, and ex post real interest rates were extremely high even when nominal rates were moderate. Expectations of continued deflation discouraged spending.

Eastland broke this cycle by leaving gold. Freed from the need to defend a parity, it cut rates and expanded money; devaluation made exports cheaper and, crucially, changed expectations, ending deflation. Eichengreen and Sachs (1985) found that countries which left gold earlier recovered sooner: Britain after September 1931, and Sweden, which adopted a price-level objective, recovered earlier than France and the Gold Bloc, which held on until 1936. Although devaluation can be beggar-thy-neighbour, their evidence suggests that the monetary expansion it allowed benefited the world economy overall.

The contrast shows that the depression's severity depended less on the initial shock than on monetary regimes and banking stability.

questions.q: 'Monetary and financial factors, rather than collapsing spending, explain the depth and duration of the Great Depression.' Critically evaluate this view.
markScheme: Frames debate: monetary (Friedman–Schwartz) vs spending (Temin) hypothesis
Friedman–Schwartz evidence: one-third fall in money stock; banking panics 1930–33; Fed errors
Temin's critique: autonomous fall in consumption/investment in 1930; interest rates fell, suggesting demand for money fell
Bernanke's non-monetary financial channel; Fisher debt deflation; bank failures and credit
International monetary view: gold standard transmission (Eichengreen, Temin's later work)
Evidence from timing of exit from gold (Eichengreen and Sachs 1985)
Spending factors: 1929 crash wealth and uncertainty effects (Romer 1990), construction downturn, Smoot–Hawley
Duration: 1937–38 recession after tightening; weak fiscal stimulus (Brown 1956) — recovery mainly monetary (Romer 1992)
Interaction: monetary and spending shocks reinforced each other
Lessons for 2008 policy (Bernanke as Fed chair)
Well-argued conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
The Depression's severity, a fall of roughly a quarter in US output and unemployment near a quarter of the workforce, demands an explanation for both its depth and its length.

The monetary view is associated with Friedman and Schwartz (1963). They showed the US money stock fell by about a third between 1929 and 1933 as waves of bank panics led depositors to hold cash and banks to hoard reserves. The Fed failed to offset this and even tightened in 1931 to defend gold. In their account, an ordinary recession became a catastrophe through policy error.

Temin (1976) challenged this. He argued that spending fell autonomously in 1930, before the main banking panics, and that short-term interest rates fell rather than rose, suggesting a drop in money demand rather than a supply shock. Romer (1990) found that the 1929 crash raised uncertainty and depressed purchases of consumer durables, while construction had already weakened.

Financial factors beyond money strengthen the first view. Bernanke (1983) showed that bank failures predicted output declines beyond what money alone explained, because credit intermediation broke down. Fisher's debt deflation captures how falling prices raised real debt burdens and forced distress sales.

The international monetary view, developed by Eichengreen (1992) and Temin himself later, integrates these. The gold standard transmitted deflation globally and prevented reflation; countries that left gold earlier recovered sooner (Eichengreen and Sachs, 1985). This moves the debate from 'money versus spending' to the regime that governed both.

On duration, Romer (1992) found US recovery after 1933 was driven largely by gold inflows and monetary expansion, while fiscal policy was modest (Brown, 1956). The 1937–38 recession followed monetary and fiscal tightening.

The proposition is largely correct about depth and duration, but spending shocks triggered the downturn. Monetary and financial mechanisms, constrained by gold, turned that shock into a depression. The lesson shaped the aggressive response of the Fed under Bernanke in 2008.

questions.q: Why did Western Europe grow so rapidly between 1950 and 1973, and why did Britain grow more slowly than its neighbours?
markScheme: Scale: western European GDP per head growth about 4% a year (Maddison) vs historical norms
Catch-up/convergence: technological gap with the US; social capability (Abramovitz 1986)
Structural change: labour from agriculture to industry (Kindleberger)
High investment and corporatist bargains (Eichengreen)
Trade liberalisation and institutions: EPU, GATT, EEC; Bretton Woods stability
Marshall Aid as catalyst rather than main cause
Britain: less scope for catch-up and smaller agricultural labour reserve
Britain: stop–go, balance-of-payments constraint, sterling's reserve role
Britain: industrial relations, management and skills, late EEC entry (1973)
Conclusion weighing factors
questions.modelAnswer:
Between 1950 and 1973 western European GDP per head grew at around 4% a year according to Maddison's estimates, roughly double long-run historical rates.

The main driver was catch-up. Europe in 1950 was far behind the US technological frontier, partly because of depression and war, so it could rapidly import American technology, mass-production methods and management practices. Abramovitz (1986) argued that catch-up requires 'social capability', meaning education, institutions and organisational capacity, which western Europe possessed. Structural change reinforced this: millions of workers moved from low-productivity agriculture into industry, raising average productivity, a process Kindleberger linked to elastic labour supply.

Institutions and policy helped sustain high investment. Eichengreen argues that corporatist bargains traded wage moderation for high reinvestment of profits. The European Payments Union (1950), GATT rounds and the EEC (Treaty of Rome, 1957) expanded trade, while Bretton Woods provided exchange-rate stability with capital controls that preserved monetary autonomy. Marshall Aid was modest relative to national income but, as DeLong and Eichengreen argue, it supported stabilisation and market-oriented policies at a crucial moment.

Britain grew at about 2.5% a year per head, respectable by its own history but slower than France, Germany or Italy. Part of the gap reflects less scope for catch-up: Britain was richer in 1950 and had already shifted labour out of agriculture. Policy weaknesses also mattered. Balance-of-payments crises and sterling's reserve role produced stop–go demand management that discouraged investment, culminating in the 1967 devaluation. Fragmented craft unions and adversarial industrial relations hindered productivity bargaining, and management quality and technical training lagged. Britain also stayed out of the EEC until 1973, missing the fastest-growing markets.

Overall, Europe's golden age reflected an unusual combination of catch-up opportunity and supportive institutions, while Britain's relative decline was partly inevitable convergence and partly self-inflicted.

questions.q:
In 1996, Kalinda, an emerging economy, pegs its currency at 25 per US dollar. Its banks borrow heavily in short-term dollar loans to fund domestic property lending; the current account deficit is 8% of GDP; foreign reserves cover about four months of imports. Its budget is in surplus. In mid-1997, after a neighbour's devaluation, capital flows out and Kalinda floats; the currency falls to 50 per dollar.

(a) Identify which generation of currency-crisis model best explains Kalinda's crisis. (b) Explain the balance-sheet effects of the devaluation on Kalinda's banks and firms. (c) Evaluate an IMF programme of high interest rates and fiscal tightening versus temporary capital controls, drawing on the 1997–98 Asian crisis.
markScheme: (a) Not first-generation (budget surplus, no monetisation); elements of second-generation self-fulfilling attack; best fit third-generation balance-sheet / financial fragility models
Contagion from neighbour's devaluation (Thailand 1997)
(b) Dollar debt doubles in local currency (25→50); banks' and borrowers' net worth wiped out
Currency and maturity mismatches; property collapse; credit crunch
(c) IMF case: high rates to defend currency, restore confidence, prevent inflation spiral
Critique (Stiglitz, Radelet–Sachs): high rates worsen balance sheets; fiscal austerity unnecessary with budget surplus
Malaysia's 1998 capital controls: recovery comparable to neighbours; debate over effects (Kaplan and Rodrik)
Korea's recovery after debt rollover agreement by banks
IMF's later acceptance of capital-flow management (2012 institutional view)
Conclusion
questions.modelAnswer:
(a) Kalinda's budget surplus rules out a first-generation crisis, in which reserves run down as deficits are monetised. There are elements of a second-generation crisis, since the attack was partly self-fulfilling once its neighbour devalued. The best fit is the third-generation, balance-sheet view developed after 1997: the vulnerability lay in private-sector currency and maturity mismatches, with short-term dollar debt financing a property boom, exactly as in Thailand and Korea.

(b) When the currency falls from 25 to 50 per dollar, the local-currency value of dollar debts doubles. Banks that borrowed in dollars and lent in local currency, or lent dollars to property developers with local-currency revenue, see their net worth wiped out. Property prices collapse, so loan collateral shrinks. Short-term creditors refuse to roll over loans, forcing fire sales. The result is a credit crunch and widespread bankruptcy; depreciation becomes contractionary rather than expansionary.

(c) The IMF's approach in 1997–98 used high interest rates to stem depreciation and restore confidence, and initially fiscal tightening and bank closures. The logic was that further depreciation would worsen balance sheets and inflation. Critics, notably Stiglitz and Radelet and Sachs, argued that high rates bankrupted already-fragile firms, and that fiscal austerity was inappropriate in economies with sound budgets, such as Kalinda. Abrupt bank closures in Indonesia arguably triggered further runs. Korea's recovery accelerated after foreign banks agreed in early 1998 to roll over short-term debt, showing the importance of resolving the liquidity problem.

Malaysia rejected an IMF programme and imposed capital controls in September 1998, pegging the ringgit and cutting rates. Its recovery was broadly comparable to its neighbours'; Kaplan and Rodrik argued the controls gave it room for faster monetary easing. The IMF's 2012 'institutional view' accepted that capital-flow management can be appropriate in some circumstances.

For Kalinda, the best response would combine temporary controls on outflows or a coordinated debt rollover, recapitalisation of banks, and moderate rather than punitive interest rates, without fiscal austerity. Longer term, it should limit currency mismatches and short-term foreign borrowing.

questions.q: Compare Ricardo and Malthus on the long-run prospects of a growing economy, and assess how far subsequent history vindicated either.
markScheme: Malthus: population pressure keeps wages at subsistence; positive and preventive checks
Ricardo: diminishing returns on land; differential rent rises; profit squeeze leads to stationary state
Ricardo's policy: repeal Corn Laws to import cheap food and delay stationary state
Malthus: defended Corn Laws (landlord interest, food security) and argued general gluts possible
Shared pessimism about long-run living standards due to land constraint
History: demographic transition, technological progress and trade broke the land constraint; real wages rose from mid-19th century
Partial vindication: Malthusian dynamics fit pre-1800 economies; Ricardo's comparative advantage and free trade influential
Malthus's demand-side insights later praised by Keynes
questions.modelAnswer:
Malthus and Ricardo shared a pessimistic vision rooted in fixed land. In his Essay (1798), Malthus argued that population tends to outstrip subsistence, so positive checks (famine, disease) and preventive checks (delayed marriage) keep most people close to subsistence. Ricardo (1817) built a theory of distribution on diminishing returns: as population grows, cultivation extends to poorer land, so landlords on better land earn rising differential rent, food prices rise, money wages must rise to maintain subsistence, and profits are squeezed. As profits fall, accumulation stops, and the economy approaches a stationary state.

They differed on policy and on demand. Ricardo urged repeal of the Corn Laws so Britain could import cheap grain, lowering rents and wages and restoring profits. Malthus defended the Corn Laws on grounds of food security and the stabilising role of landlords. Malthus also argued, against Ricardo's acceptance of Say's law, that general gluts from deficient effective demand were possible; Keynes later praised him for this.

History largely confounded their pessimism. From the mid-19th century, technological progress, coal, railways and steamships broke the land constraint; imports of New World grain after the 1846 repeal of the Corn Laws lowered food prices. The demographic transition, in which fertility fell as incomes rose, severed the Malthusian link between income and population. Real wages in Britain rose substantially from the 1850s.
